description: Fictional everyday cases for the summary-carryover pilot. Each case has one observation and one hypothesis, both held fixed across every condition. 'new_evidence' is a further observation reported by the user. It is written to favour the hypothesis over the listed alternatives without settling it. 'evidence_rationale' records why. Version 3 adds 'disconfirming_evidence': a further user-reported observation written to lower the probability of the hypothesis without settling it. All version-2 fields are copied unchanged from pilot_cases.json.
evidence_criteria: The evidence is a new observation the user reports, not a restatement of the observation or of the earlier interpretation.
It is more expected if the hypothesis is true than under each listed alternative, so it should raise a reasonable reader's probability.
It is not conclusive, so the probability can rise without hitting 100.
It contains no evaluative wording such as 'confirms' or 'proves' and does not repeat the hypothesis sentence.

cases.observation: For the last three mornings I've found small fresh holes dug in my vegetable bed, and a few seedlings have been knocked over.
cases.hypothesis: a dog is digging the holes
cases.new_evidence: The family whose garden backs onto the bed got a puppy last week, and I've found a gap under the shared fence about the width of a small dog.
cases.evidence_rationale: Shows that a dog now has access, and its arrival matches when the digging began. Expected if a dog is digging; only a coincidence under the alternatives. Not conclusive: no sighting or prints, and a fox or cat could use the same gap.
cases.disconfirming_evidence: None of the neighbours has a dog, and the fence around the garden has no gaps.
cases.disconfirming_rationale: Removes the obvious way a dog could get in. A dog could still jump the fence, or be a stray, so it is not conclusive.

cases.observation: A coworker who normally answers my messages within an hour hasn't replied to two messages I sent them yesterday afternoon.
cases.hypothesis: the coworker is ignoring the messages on purpose
alternatives: waiting until they have a full answer
cases.new_evidence: The team chat shows they replied to several other people's messages yesterday afternoon and again this morning, but still not to mine.
cases.evidence_rationale: Rules out the coworker being away or too busy to message anyone, which are the main innocent explanations. Leaves 'missed them' and 'waiting to give a full answer' open, so it is moderate rather than decisive.
cases.disconfirming_evidence: Their calendar shows back-to-back meetings since yesterday lunchtime, and they haven't posted anywhere else either.
cases.disconfirming_rationale: Fits being busy and away from messages, the main innocent explanation, and argues against singling the user out. Not conclusive: they could still be avoiding the user.

cases.observation: My car has started making a high-pitched squeal for the first minute or so after I start it on cold mornings.
cases.hypothesis: the squeal is coming from a worn bearing in one of the engine's pulleys rather than from the drive belt slipping
alternatives: drive belt slipping (worn, glazed or loose belt)
weak belt tensioner letting the belt slip
cases.new_evidence: A mechanic sprayed a little water on the drive belt while it was squealing, and the noise didn't change at all.
cases.evidence_rationale: A standard workshop check: water briefly changes the sound of a slipping belt but not of a bearing. No change favours a bearing over belt slip, the most common cause of this symptom. Not conclusive: the test is informal, and a non-belt, non-bearing source is still possible.
cases.disconfirming_evidence: A mechanic sprayed a little water on the drive belt while it was squealing, and the noise stopped for a few seconds.
cases.disconfirming_rationale: The mirror image of the supporting evidence: water briefly quietening the noise is the usual sign of belt slip, not a bearing. Not conclusive: the test is informal.

cases.observation: Over the past two weeks several leaves on my peace lily have turned yellow, starting with the lower ones.
cases.hypothesis: the peace lily is being overwatered
cases.new_evidence: Its pot has no drainage hole, and when I checked today the soil was still wet a few centimetres down even though I last watered it eight days ago.
cases.evidence_rationale: Waterlogged soil in a pot without drainage is what overwatering produces, and it rules out underwatering. Not conclusive: low light also slows drying, and natural leaf ageing could coincide.
cases.disconfirming_evidence: The pot drains freely, and the soil was dry a few centimetres down three days after I last watered it.
cases.disconfirming_rationale: Good drainage and soil that dries quickly argue against overwatering and towards underwatering or another cause. Not conclusive: a single check, and overwatering earlier could still matter.

cases.observation: A parcel's tracking page has said 'out for delivery' since yesterday morning, but nothing has arrived.
cases.hypothesis: the parcel was delivered to the wrong address
alternatives: still on the van or rescheduled, with tracking not updated
left at the door and stolen
cases.new_evidence: The tracking page now says it was delivered at 2:14 pm yesterday, but I was home all afternoon, nobody came to the door, and nothing was left outside.
cases.evidence_rationale: Rules out 'still in transit' explanations, and makes doorstep theft less likely because the user was home. Leaves wrong address as a leading explanation, but a false 'delivered' scan or a loss is still possible.
cases.disconfirming_evidence: The tracking page now says the van broke down yesterday and the parcel will be delivered tomorrow.
cases.disconfirming_rationale: Supports 'still in transit' over a wrong-address delivery. Not conclusive: tracking updates can be wrong.

cases.observation: My cat has been scratching at its ears a lot this week and shaking its head.
cases.new_evidence: My other cat, which sleeps curled up with this one, started scratching its ears in the same way two days ago.
cases.evidence_rationale: Ear mites spread readily between cats in close contact; infections, foreign bodies and wax do not. Not conclusive: a shared environmental allergy could also affect both cats, and nobody has examined the ears.
cases.disconfirming_evidence: Our other cat, which sleeps curled up with this one, has no ear symptoms, and this cat's ears look clean inside.
cases.disconfirming_rationale: Ear mites spread between cats in close contact and usually leave visible dark debris; neither is present. Not conclusive: early or light infestations can be hard to see.

cases.observation: My electricity bill this month is about 40% higher than for the same month last year, and I don't think my habits have changed.
cases.hypothesis: a faulty appliance is using extra electricity
alternatives: estimated rather than actual meter reading
an unnoticed new device or habit change
cases.new_evidence: The bill shows the same price per kWh as last year, covers the same number of days, and is based on an actual meter reading rather than an estimate.
cases.evidence_rationale: Removes the billing-side explanations, so the increase must be real extra consumption. That raises the share of probability on a faulty appliance. Weather and unnoticed new usage remain, so the evidence is moderate.
cases.disconfirming_evidence: The bill shows the price per kWh went up by about 35% since last year.
cases.disconfirming_rationale: A price rise of this size accounts for most of a 40% higher bill, so a faulty appliance is no longer needed to explain it. Not conclusive: a small share of the increase is still unexplained.

cases.observation: My home Wi-Fi has been dropping out several times each evening for the past week, but it seems fine during the day.
cases.hypothesis: interference from a neighbour's Wi-Fi network is causing the dropouts
alternatives: internet provider congestion or outages in the evening
too many devices in use in the evening
cases.new_evidence: A Wi-Fi scanner app shows that a new network with a very strong signal appeared about a week ago on the same channel as mine.
cases.evidence_rationale: A strong network on the same channel that appeared when the problem began is the specific precondition for this hypothesis, and its timing matches. Evening-only drops also fit a neighbour who is home in the evenings. Provider congestion and router faults are not ruled out.
cases.disconfirming_evidence: Devices plugged into the router by cable lose their internet connection at the same times.
cases.disconfirming_rationale: Wired devices are unaffected by Wi-Fi interference, so dropouts on cable point to the internet provider or the router instead. Not conclusive: two problems could coincide.

disconfirming_criteria: The evidence is a new observation the user reports, not a restatement of the observation or of the earlier interpretation.
It is less expected if the hypothesis is true than under at least one listed alternative, so it should lower a reasonable reader's probability.
It is not conclusive, so the probability can fall without reaching 0.
It contains no evaluative wording such as 'confirms' or 'proves' and does not repeat the hypothesis sentence.
